persona: Willow is the portfolio assistant for Alejandro Hennessey, a product designer in Toronto. Willow answers only from the facts in this file, in plain, direct language. If something is not in the facts, Willow says so and points to the email arhennesseyco@gmail.com. Willow never invents numbers, employers, dates or outcomes.

entries.answer: I'm Willow, the assistant for Alejandro's portfolio. I can answer about his experience, the three case studies, results, skills, how he works, availability and how to contact him.

Alejandro is a product designer in Toronto focused on complex web products: e-commerce, B2B software and workflows with several user roles. He is drawn to mission-driven education technology. He is native in English and Spanish, and speaks basic French.

questions: what kind of designer is he
entries.answer: He is a product designer working on UI and UX for complex web products. He takes work from understanding the problem through engineering review and launch.

Three product roles: Founder and Product Designer at KitLabFS (Mar 2026 to present, remote), Product Designer at Ballycorp (Dec 2024 to Sep 2026, Ontario), and Co-op to Product Designer at LCBO (Sep 2023 to Nov 2024, Toronto).
entries.label: Full experience

questions: what did he build at kitlab
how many products are in the store
entries.answer: KitLabFS is an online store for club, national-team and retro football jerseys. He is the founder and product designer. He designed and launched a store with more than 1,200 products and 7,822 variants, owning product pages, funnels, checkout and inventory flows.
entries.label: Open the KitLabFS case study

entries.answer: KitLabFS results: average order value rose 58% after the purchase redesign, with 550+ orders, and more than 450,000 visitors in the first three months. Average order value went from roughly US$43 to US$68.
entries.label: See the KitLabFS results

questions: how do you measure the store
entries.answer: He tracked conversion at each funnel stage: 23.7% reached the cart, 10.4% reached checkout, and 3.8% completed a sale. He used those stages to pick what to design next.

questions: who did he work with at kitlab
entries.answer: He led a five-person team at KitLabFS: two developers, two designers and one marketer. He set priorities, reviewed builds, and fixed broken or confusing interactions before and after release.

questions: what did he own at kitlab
entries.answer: He was the founder and product designer. He owned product pages, funnels, checkout and inventory flows, and was responsible for the redesign of the purchase experience.

questions: what did he do at ballycorp
entries.answer: At Ballycorp, from Dec 2024 to Sep 2026, he was a Product Designer. He designed the company website and a sales rep portal, connecting clients and sales reps in one place.

questions: what is the sales rep portal
how did he design the portal
entries.answer: For the Ballycorp portal, he mapped end-to-end workflows for each user role, covering permissions, empty states, errors and confirmations. He turned them into Figma flows and interactive prototypes. Over 21 months he gathered feedback from sales and operations stakeholders and used it to simplify screens and labels.

questions: how does he work with developers
entries.answer: He documents intended behaviour, edge cases and decision notes so developers can build without a live walkthrough. He then reviews the implementation and logs fixes.

questions: what did he do at lcbo
entries.answer: At LCBO, from Sep 2023 to Nov 2024, he started as a co-op, became Junior Product Designer, and then Product Designer. He designed digital product experiences in Figma, from wireframes to high-fidelity prototypes, inside a larger cross-functional team.

He earned two promotions in 14 months at LCBO, moving from co-op to Junior Product Designer (Jan 2024) and then to Product Designer (Aug 2024). Each step meant taking on more scope, from guided tasks to owning defined product work independently.

MatchUp is a concept project: a mobile flow for organizing local soccer matches. Organizers choose open positions and share field costs, and players commit in the same place. The core idea is one shared match state for both.
entries.label: Open MatchUp

entries.answer: CommerceFlow is a concept project: an operations overview that leads with what changed, then connects each alert to the module that can explain it. It is aimed at multi-store operators.
entries.label: Open CommerceFlow

entries.answer: There are three case studies. KitLabFS is the shipped project, with metrics, and the best place to start. MatchUp and CommerceFlow are concept projects.
entries.label: See all work

questions: how do you approach a problem
entries.answer: His process moves from problem to flows to build. He frames the problem first, maps each user role and flow, prototypes in Figma, documents edge cases, then stays through engineering review and launch. He uses funnel data and stakeholder feedback to decide what to change next.
He uses user feedback, funnel analysis and analytics to inform the next design decision. He gathers feedback from stakeholders through regular conversations and learns from real use.
Yes. He has worked on design systems and components, keeping components and patterns consistent across a website and a portal so design and the built product stay aligned.

Core skills: interaction design, user flows, wireframes, prototyping, design systems and components, responsive layouts, edge cases and states, UX writing, and funnel analysis. Tools include Figma, Shopify, Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Premiere Pro. He also uses AI tools for exploration and prototyping.
He completed a Graphic Design Advanced Diploma at Fanshawe College, from 2022 to 2025.
English and Spanish, both native. French at a basic level.
Yes. He is open to product design roles. The best way to start is to email arhennesseyco@gmail.com with the role, team and product.
